questions.title: How exactly do exponential input/forget gates enable “revising” stored values in sLSTM?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that standard LSTMs struggle to revise storage decisions (e.g., in the Nearest Neighbor Search toy task), and that sLSTM fixes this via exponential gating. In equations (Eq. 11–17 for sLSTM), the update is still additive: $c_t = f_t c_{t-1} + i_t z_t$, but now $i_t = \exp(\tilde{i}_t)$ and $f_t \in \{\sigma(\tilde{f}_t), \exp(\tilde{f}_t)\}$. Intuitively, how does switching from sigmoid to exponential produce the ability to overwrite or revise earlier content? Is the key that $i_t$ can become arbitrarily large (compared to the bounded $\sigma$), thus dominating $f_t c_{t-1}$? If so, how is numerical stability preserved beyond the normalizer $n_t$ and stabilizer $m_t$? A small worked example showing where a later, more-similar vector replaces an earlier stored vector would help.

questions.title: What is the precise role of the normalizer state $n_t$ in sLSTM and why does $h_t$ divide by it?
questions.question_body: In sLSTM, the normalizer evolves as $n_t = f_t n_{t-1} + i_t$ and the hidden pre-output is $\tilde{h}_t = c_t / n_t$. This looks like a normalized weighted average of past inputs. Is $n_t$ theoretically justified as a partition function analog (like normalizing attention weights), or is it more of a numerical stabilization device because $i_t$ can be unbounded? Under what conditions can $n_t$ approach zero, and is that prevented by the same stabilizer $m_t$ trick? Could $n_t$ be interpreted as an exact sum of weights $\prod_{s'=s+1}^t f_{s'}$ applied to each past input weight $i_s$?

questions.title: Why does replacing $(i_t, f_t)$ with their stabilized versions $(i'_t, f'_t)$ not change outputs or gradients?
questions.question_body: Equations (18–20) introduce a stabilizer state $m_t$ and define $i'_t = \exp(\log i_t - m_t)$ and $f'_t = \exp(\log f_t + m_{t-1} - m_t)$. The paper states (Appendix referenced) that using $(i'_t, f'_t)$ in place of $(i_t, f_t)$ leaves both the forward outputs and the loss gradients w.r.t. parameters unchanged. Could someone sketch the proof? Is it because $m_t$ factors out as a common rescaling over all accumulated terms in $c_t$ and $n_t$, which subsequently cancels in $\tilde{h}_t$ due to division by $n_t$ (and similarly in backprop)? A concise derivation would help.

questions.title: How is the mLSTM normalizer $\mathbf{n}_t$ used for division, and what is the effect of the absolute value and threshold?
questions.question_body: In mLSTM, $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t / \max\{ |\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t|, 1\}$. Why do we divide by the scalar $\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t$ (absolute value) rather than, e.g., a norm? What is the interpretation—are we normalizing by the accumulated gating mass projected onto the query direction to match the scale of a weighted sum like in attention? How sensitive is performance to the lower bound of 1.0, and what happens if $|\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t| \ll 1$? Does the absolute value break any desirable sign information for retrieval?

questions.title: Is the mLSTM covariance update just a form of linear attention with gating?
questions.question_body: The mLSTM update is $\mathbf{C}_t = f_t \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top$, and retrieval is $\mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t$ normalized by $\max\{|\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t|, 1\}$. This strongly resembles linearized attention with features $\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$ (no kernel), learning rate $i_t$, and decay $f_t$. Is mLSTM functionally equivalent to a gated linear attention mechanism plus an output gate $\mathbf{o}_t$? If not, what key differences remain (e.g., use of absolute value in normalization, per-step scalar gates vs per-head/token gates)?

questions.title: Why are multiple heads and multiple cells equivalent in mLSTM but not in sLSTM?
questions.question_body: The paper states that for mLSTM, multiple heads and multiple cells are equivalent since there is no memory mixing, but for sLSTM heads introduce a new way of memory mixing (within head, across cells). Could someone formalize this? If we have $H$ heads with independent matrix memories $\{\mathbf{C}^{(h)}\}_{h=1}^H$ and concatenate their outputs, how is that equivalent to having $H$ separate cells? In sLSTM, how exactly does head-level isolation prevent cross-head mixing while allowing within-head recurrent mixing across cells via $\mathbf{R}_\bullet$?

questions.title: Parallelization of mLSTM: what is the exact scan/associative formulation?
questions.question_body: The paper claims mLSTM is fully parallelizable (like FlashAttention or GLA) and refers to an appendix for a parallel form. Given $\mathbf{C}_t = f_t \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top$ and $\mathbf{n}_t = f_t \mathbf{n}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{k}_t$, can someone write the exact associative operator that enables a parallel prefix scan over time? Is it a semiring over pairs $(\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{n})$ with a time-varying scalar $f_t$? A concrete expression showing how to combine two segments' summaries into one would clarify implementation.

questions.title: Computational complexity of mLSTM’s matrix memory: is the $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ cost per token unavoidable?
questions.question_body: Each step updates and applies a $d \times d$ matrix $\mathbf{C}_t$, implying $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ compute and memory traffic per token. Are there structured parameterizations or low-rank approximations consistent with the covariance update (e.g., maintaining $R$ rank-1 terms with decays) that preserve the claimed properties (gating, normalization, parallelization) while reducing cost to $\mathcal{O}(dR)$? If so, what is lost in terms of capacity or retrieval fidelity versus full-rank $\mathbf{C}_t$?

questions.title: How critical is the zero-mean assumption for keys/values in the covariance update rule?
questions.question_body: The paper assumes LayerNorm before key/value projections so that keys/values have zero mean, then cites optimality properties of the covariance rule. What breaks if the mean-shift is nonzero (e.g., due to learned biases or distribution drift)? Does a nonzero mean introduce a spurious rank-1 component that degrades retrieval via increased cross-talk? Would explicit mean-centering per batch or per sequence be preferable to relying on LayerNorm?

questions.title: Does exponential forgetting $f_t = \exp(\tilde{f}_t)$ preserve the ‘constant error carousel’ property?
questions.question_body: Classic LSTM avoids vanishing gradients partly because $c_t$ accumulates additively with $f_t \in (0,1)$ typically near 1. With $f_t = \exp(\tilde{f}_t)$, $f_t$ can be greater than 1 or much smaller than 1. How does this affect gradient flow through time in $c_t$ or $\mathbf{C}_t$? Are there initialization or regularization strategies (e.g., biasing $\tilde{f}_t$) that ensure effective long-range credit assignment without exploding/vanishing due to $\prod f_t$? The Limitations section mentions careful initialization—what concretely works in practice?

questions.title: Why is $\mathbf{k}_t$ scaled by $1/\sqrt{d}$ but $\mathbf{q}_t$ and $\mathbf{v}_t$ are not in mLSTM?
questions.question_body: In Eq. (26–28), $\mathbf{k}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_k$, but no similar scaling is shown for $\mathbf{q}_t$ or $\mathbf{v}_t$. Is this analogous to dot-product attention where scaling the key (or query) stabilizes the magnitude of inner products? Given that retrieval uses $\mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t$ normalized by $\max\{|\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t|,1\}$, how sensitive is training to whether we scale keys, queries, both, or neither?

questions.title: How does sLSTM ‘memory mixing’ make it more expressive than SSMs/Transformers for state tracking?
questions.question_body: The paper cites results that SSMs and Transformers lack state-tracking capacity akin to RNNs, and argues sLSTM’s memory mixing (recurrent $\mathbf{R}_\bullet$ across cells within heads) plus exponential gating enables solving formal language tasks like parity. Can someone give a minimal constructive example showing sLSTM’s recurrent mixing implements a finite-state machine that Transformers/SSMs cannot, even with large capacity? How do heads restrict or enhance this expressivity?

questions.title: What is the theoretical memory capacity of mLSTM compared to attention’s exponential capacity in $d$?
questions.question_body: The paper notes Transformers have memory that is exponential in coding dimension $d$. For mLSTM, with a $d \times d$ unparameterized memory updated by rank-1 outer products, what is the asymptotic capacity for storing and reliably retrieving $N$ random key-value pairs under noise and interference? Is there a closed-form or known bound (e.g., akin to Hopfield or modern associative memory analyses), especially when $i_t$ and $f_t$ vary over time?

questions.title: Post vs pre up-projection choice: is there a principled reason sLSTM uses post and mLSTM uses pre?
questions.question_body: The xLSTM block uses post up-projection for sLSTM and pre up-projection for mLSTM, motivated by Cover’s theorem and the idea that mLSTM benefits from larger memory in high-dimensional space. Is there an ablation that isolates this choice from other factors? Theoretically, does placing mLSTM after an up-projection maximize separability by letting the matrix memory live in a higher-dimensional manifold, whereas sLSTM benefits from summarizing first in the base space? Any guidance for practitioners choosing between them?

questions.title: How fair are the throughput and generation-time comparisons given implementation maturity?
questions.question_body: The paper reports throughput/generation-time comparisons where xLSTM is competitive and notes that their mLSTM CUDA kernels are not yet optimized, while FlashAttention and Mamba scans are highly optimized. Also, some models could not be compiled with torch.compile in the test environment. How should we interpret the reported speedups or slowdowns under these constraints? Could the authors provide a normalized FLOPs-based comparison or a breakdown isolating the $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ matrix-memory cost vs other layers to help predict performance after kernel optimization?

questions.title: Ablation clarity: how much gain comes from exponential gates vs matrix memory vs backbone changes?
questions.question_body: The ablations progressively morph a vanilla LSTM into xLSTM by adding pre-LayerNorm residual backbones, up-projection blocks, exponential gating, and matrix memory. Could someone quantify the incremental perplexity improvements attributable to each change in isolation? For example: vanilla LSTM in residual block (no exp gates), then add exp gates only, then add matrix memory only, then both. This would help separate gains due to training stabilization/backbone from genuine modeling advances (exp gates, mLSTM).

questions.title: Why is memory mixing prohibited across sLSTM heads but allowed across cells within a head?
questions.question_body: The text says sLSTM can have multiple heads with memory mixing across cells within each head, but not across heads. Is this a design constraint to avoid instabilities with exponential gates (e.g., runaway amplification if cross-head mixing occurred), or an efficiency/parallelism consideration? Mathematically, what would break if we allowed $\mathbf{R}_\bullet$ to connect cells across heads as well? Any empirical evidence that cross-head mixing hurts performance?

questions.title: On length extrapolation: what prevents mLSTM’s matrix memory from saturating at very long contexts?
questions.question_body: The paper notes a potential limitation: the matrix memory is independent of sequence length, so longer sequences might overload it. Yet experiments show good perplexity up to 16k context. Can someone explain the factors that mitigate saturation—e.g., decay via $f_t$, normalization by $\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t$, or the statistics of natural language? Is there a diagnostic to detect when interference grows too large (e.g., retrieval norm growth, cosine with true value falling below a threshold), and a mitigation like adaptive forgetting?
